correction: -18 dBFS is sometimes used as an average/reference orientation, not a universal peak target.
myth: Every track should peak at exactly -18 dBFS.
safer_principle: Use source dynamics and each processor’s documented operating level.

correction: Waveform size is not sound quality; clipped capture cannot be repaired by turning down later.
myth: The waveform must be large to sound professional.
safer_principle: Record cleanly with real converter headroom and monitor louder if needed.

correction: Modern 24-bit capture allows generous headroom without sacrificing practical quality.
myth: 24-bit recording needs peaks near 0 dBFS.
safer_principle: Prioritize unclipped performance and a healthy real-world noise floor.

correction: The fader may be after inserts and may not change processor input.
myth: A lower fader fixes overdriven plug-ins upstream.
safer_principle: Move gain at the stage that should react differently.

correction: Calibration and headroom behavior are product-specific.
myth: All analog-model plug-ins are calibrated to exactly -18 dBFS.
safer_principle: Read the manual and level-match conservative/hotter passes.

correction: Converters, nonlinear plug-ins, fixed stages, buses, and physical outputs still have limits or level-dependent behavior.
myth: Floating point means gain staging never matters.
safer_principle: Trace the whole chain and distinguish mathematical headroom from processor/output behavior.

correction: A red internal meter may be a warning in a floating-point stage, but the exact stage matters.
myth: Red on any internal channel means the file is destroyed.
safer_principle: Find the first clipping/nonlinear/output stage.

correction: It only changes a later stage and may conceal upstream overload.
myth: Turning down the master fader repairs clipping everywhere.
safer_principle: Reduce the earliest responsible stage.

correction: Auto-gain behavior may be approximate and program-dependent.
myth: Auto Gain always makes fair A/B comparisons.
safer_principle: Verify with meters and ears at matched perceived loudness.

correction: They are accurate for a different point in the chain.
myth: Pre-fader meters are always more accurate.
safer_principle: Choose meter position based on the question.

correction: Normalization can erase useful relationships and alter nonlinear processor input.
myth: Normalize every file before mixing.
safer_principle: Use intentional region/trim gain when needed.

correction: It also controls nonlinear response, detector behavior, noise, sends, and fader usability.
myth: Gain staging is only about avoiding clipping.
safer_principle: Manage each stage for predictable processing.

correction: Within practical 24-bit/floating workflows, moderate digital attenuation is recoverable.
myth: A quiet digital track has permanently lost detail.
safer_principle: Distinguish digital level from analog noise and capture quality.

correction: Monitor level normally changes playback loudness, not file level.
myth: The monitor knob changes the mix signal.
safer_principle: Use monitoring for listening comfort and gain controls for signal level.

correction: A bus is the routing path and the aux is typically the receiving channel strip.
myth: A bus and an aux are two unrelated things in Logic.
safer_principle: Trace source output/send, bus destination, and aux output.

correction: A send normally creates a parallel feed while the dry path continues.
myth: A send creates a subgroup.
safer_principle: Use output-to-bus routing for a true subgroup.

correction: Folder and Summing Stacks have different signal-flow behavior.
myth: Folder Stack processing affects all subtracks like a Summing Stack.
safer_principle: Use Summing Stack/aux when shared audio processing is required.

correction: Shared compression is useful only if its gain movement supports the music.
myth: Every group needs compression for glue.
safer_principle: Level-match bypass and listen for cohesion versus flattening.

correction: It can also blur attacks, add harshness, and reduce separation.
myth: Bus saturation always makes tracks feel like one thing.
safer_principle: Drive subtly and judge dense sections at matched loudness.

correction: Bus EQ changes every member, including those not causing the problem.
myth: Bus EQ is always more musical than source EQ.
safer_principle: Fix scope first.

correction: A VCA controls members; an aux receives and processes summed audio.
myth: VCA and aux faders do the same thing.
safer_principle: Choose control versus signal flow.

correction: Parallel paths add processed energy and can still reduce contrast or cause phase problems.
myth: Parallel compression preserves dynamics automatically.
safer_principle: Level-match total output and check phase.

correction: Unity is convenient but not a law; stage placement and automation matter.
myth: The bus fader should always stay at 0 dB.
safer_principle: Document baseline and keep useful control range.

correction: Deep routing can obscure gain, latency, and ownership.
myth: Nested buses are always more professional.
safer_principle: Use the simplest hierarchy that serves the mix.

correction: Rooms, parallel paths, samples, or special effects may need different routing.
myth: All drums belong on the same bus.
safer_principle: Define membership by desired shared processing.

correction: Lead and support roles may require separate control.
myth: All vocals should share one bus chain.
safer_principle: Preserve hierarchy before cohesion.

correction: Useful gain reduction is program- and goal-dependent.
myth: A bus compressor should show a fixed amount of gain reduction.
safer_principle: Listen to groove, transients, and detector control.

correction: Solo hides masking, hierarchy, and total loudness.
myth: If the bus sounds better solo, it is better in the mix.
safer_principle: Judge bus processing in context.

correction: Peak measures instantaneous extrema; perceived loudness depends on energy and weighting over time.
myth: Peak level tells you perceived loudness.
safer_principle: Use the right meter and listening context.

correction: LUFS does not replace peak/true-peak control.
myth: LUFS prevents clipping.
safer_principle: Measure loudness and peaks separately.

correction: They use different weighting, gating, and standards.
myth: RMS and LUFS are identical.
safer_principle: Use RMS for simple energy orientation and LUFS for standardized loudness.

correction: Integrated loudness depends on the measured programme range.
myth: Integrated LUFS from a chorus loop represents the full song.
safer_principle: Measure the full intended range.

correction: LRA describes macro loudness variation and is unreliable for some short content.
myth: LRA is a punch meter.
safer_principle: Use crest/envelope listening for local punch.

correction: Inter-sample/true peaks may exceed sample peaks.
myth: 0 dBFS sample peaks guarantee no clipping after conversion.
safer_principle: Use true-peak metering when delivery requires it.

correction: Limiting changes peaks, envelope, distortion, and often stereo behavior.
myth: A limiter makes audio loud without changing it.
safer_principle: Level-match and listen to the removed dynamics.

correction: It cannot reconstruct clipped input samples.
myth: A limiter repairs clipped recordings.
safer_principle: Prevent converter clipping or repair source separately.

correction: True-peak and encoding behavior may require margin.
myth: A limiter ceiling of 0 dB is always safest.
safer_principle: Choose ceiling for delivery and verify after the final stage.

correction: It still changes waveform and harmonics.
myth: Soft clipping is transparent.
safer_principle: Use the smallest amount that survives level-matched comparison.

correction: Small controlled clipping can be a deliberate peak-control choice.
myth: Hard clipping is always unusable.
safer_principle: Judge amount, oversampling, material, and downstream peaks.

correction: Excess limiting can remove transient contrast and make normalized playback smaller.
myth: More LUFS always sounds more powerful.
safer_principle: Compare at matched playback loudness.

correction: Playback normalization targets are not universal mastering mandates.
myth: Streaming services require masters at exactly -14 LUFS.
safer_principle: Master for quality and destination, then measure.

correction: It is an estimate of playback gain adjustment.
myth: A loudness penalty is a quality score.
safer_principle: Judge audio after level normalization.

correction: It depends on window, source, and arrangement.
myth: Crest factor alone measures dynamic quality.
safer_principle: Combine metrics with listening.

correction: Arrangement and intent differ.
myth: Dynamic range should be the same in every genre.
safer_principle: Preserve useful contrast for the specific work.

correction: It can alter sound and may be unnecessary in some private/internal contexts.
myth: True-peak limiting should always be on.
safer_principle: Use it when destination risk justifies it.

correction: It redistributes peak-control artifacts.
myth: Clipping before limiting creates free loudness.
safer_principle: Compare limiter-only and staged control at equal loudness.

correction: Multiple stages can help or accumulate damage.
myth: Several limiters are automatically cleaner than one.
safer_principle: Measure total reduction and listen to the chain.

correction: Source envelope, note balance, arrangement, or detector filtering may be the real cause.
myth: Low-end limiter pumping is solved only by faster release.
safer_principle: Find what drives gain reduction.

correction: It can obscure transient and balance decisions.
myth: A master bus limiter should hide unfinished balance problems.
safer_principle: Fix the mix or use the limiter intentionally with awareness.

correction: There is no universal requirement when the file is unclipped and processing is documented.
myth: Mastering needs exactly -6 dBFS peak headroom.
safer_principle: Agree on delivery with the mastering engineer.

correction: True peak estimates reconstructed waveform maxima between samples.
myth: True peak and sample peak are the same thing.
safer_principle: Use appropriate true-peak metering.

correction: They represent different time windows.
myth: Momentary, short-term, and integrated loudness are interchangeable.
safer_principle: Choose the window that matches the question.

correction: Album relationships may be intentionally varied.
myth: The loudest section alone defines album loudness intent.
safer_principle: Evaluate track and album context.

correction: Monitoring level changes perception, not file meter readings.
myth: Turning up monitoring makes the master measure louder.
safer_principle: Calibrate listening separately from signal gain.

correction: Intermediate nonlinear or fixed stages may already distort.
myth: If the final meter is safe, every earlier stage is safe.
safer_principle: Meter/diagnose at the responsible stage.

correction: Tonal balance, transients, width, codecs, and arrangement still matter.
myth: If the mix meets LUFS and true peak targets, it will translate.
safer_principle: Treat delivery metrics as boundaries, not complete quality assessment.
